MASSED MARIMBA - breaking the world record for marimba players en masse

By: Marion Edmunds | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We go behind the scenes of a record-breaking mass marimba concert to find out whose making the music….

Unique Selling Point:
We have access to film the attempt to break the world record for massed marimba playing, and interview the people organising it. By telling the story of that 10-minute musical moment, we will loop back to tell the story of a successful social business, Marimba Jam, founded by Kiara Ramklass, who brings people - mostly women - together to learn and play the marimbas. The story will show how universally loved this instrument has become in South Africa, and how useful it is as a tool to create harmony and unity between different groups of people, from different backgrounds. The piece features two school girls from different ends of the socio-economic divide who experience marimbas in a way that makes them forge a common bond with others.

Summary:
On August the 2nd , 1300 marimba players, most of them school-going age, will descend on Grand West, an entertainment complex near Cape Town, in an attempt to break the record for the largest group of marimba players making music together. The Guiness Book of records for such an event was set most recently by a musical ensemble in Guatamala. https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/largest-ensemble-marimba.

What makes this 2025 effort different is that most of the players will be women or girls.
https://www.facebook.com/MarimbaJam/

This attempt to set a musical record is facilitated by an organisation called Marimba Jam – a female-driven social enterprise that teaches and performs marimbas in the Mother City. The Guinness book of records attempt creates a visual and audible focus for the Marimba movement which brings so much joy to young musicians across schools and communities in South Africa, and the world. And Marimba Jam provides the logistics to do this.

And given the demand for marimbas, we will also meet and interview the young marimba players turned manufacturers who are building instruments for the Record-breaking attempt in a new small factory in Ottery.

Here's some historical detail: the origin of Marimbas are lost in time, but they are thought to either have evolved in South East Asia in the 14th century or in Africa, and then carried with slaves from Africa to South and North America in the 16th century, globalising the instrument which has continued to develop over the centuries. https://southafrica.co.za/origins-structure-marimba.html The instrument revival in Southern Africa came in the last centuries when it was often used for worship, with churches using them as orchestras in rural settings. https://www.ru.ac.za/ilam/products/cds/davedargiecollection/

The Marimba Jam organisation was started in 2017 by a woman, Kiara Ramklass, who started playing marimba at school, not stopping through university where she used her music to make ends meet. Her organisation was an attempt to find a musical way to bridge the divide between privileged and disadvantaged schools, and to bring young people together - literally in harmony, movement and melody. Through her growing movement, she has managed to create an accredited African Marimba school curriculum, and teaches about 500 school kids weekly. They particularly focus on women – 90 per cent of their students and a hundred per cent of the teachers are females. And they have prevailed for over ten years.

The climax of the feature would be the mass Marimba jam at Grand West with a degree of suspense – will they be able to break the record? And whether they do or not, what would hundreds of marimba players together in song and movement look and sound like? But leading up to that we would profile Kiara Ramklass and two school-girls coming to the jam – one from a privileged school and one from a disadvantaged one.

We might also add to this an interview with Dizu Plaatjies, the musician who brought Marimbas from the Eastern Cape to Cape Town in 1979, having been mentored by Ethnomusicologist Dave Dargie who did a great deal to record indigenous instruments in religious settings. Plaatjies started out performing marimbas on Adderley Street as a busker, and from there, created the famous Amampondo percussion band which toured the world, including playing at the iconic Free Nelson Mandela concert in Wembley. When he introduced marimbas to Cape Town in the 1980’s, the instrument was little played, and now it’s a musical force, and part of many schools’ repertoire. If we could bring the now Professor Plaatjies to witness the jam at Grand West, the feature would be all the sweeter.
